newsitem.title: USA: US Aluminum Assn to persevere with EU tariff issue.
newsitem.headline: US Aluminum Assn to persevere with EU tariff issue.

text.p: The Aluminum Association will still pursue its goal of getting the European Union's 8.5 percent tariff on aluminum imports scrapped despite little immediate hope of U.S. trade officials taking up the cudgel.

Aluminum Association President David Parker said the French were the main block to scrapping the tariff, but for any progress to come, it was a question of getting the issue on the right international trade talk agendas at the right time.
"The stars have to align in a certain way, and so far we have not had the right alignment," Parker told Reuters. "Clearly the French position has never been to our liking."
"We have never taken this issue off the front burner," Parker said. The tariff was unfair and enough to discourage some U.S. mill products exports to the EU.
"Any opportunity we see to advance that position, we will," Parker said.
He declined to comment on recent talks with United States Trade Representative, which included the tariff issue.
The association's vice president of government relations, Barry Meyer said, "We have no problem with our government on this issue." It was U.S. policy to scrap the tariff too.
The tariff, currently at 8.5 percent, is set to fall 0.5 percent in 1998 and 1999 to a floor of 7.5 percent.
The world's biggest aluminum industry got welcome news recently when U.S. Justice Department confirmed that its anti-trust probe was now closed, with no action to be taken.
The investigation was launched following the Memorandum of Understanding signed by leading aluminum producer nations to curb the effect of Russian metal exports on Western markets.

The Aluminum Association is now looking at more pressing issues such as the environment and most recently, the surge in the dollar and rising imports of Japanese cars into the U.S. and a dip in U.S. made car sales.
"U.S. cars use more aluminum than Japanese cars," Parker noted.
Safeguarding the aluminum beverage can market is also uppermost in the association's mind, especially when canstock orders have fallen this year, the light metal's biggest single sector.
"We definitely recognize that PET (plastic) containers have made significant advances. We don't have the growth numbers we have had in the past," Parker said.
The number of actual cans produced have increased, but with technical advances, less metal is used each year to make a can.
Pechiney SA said recently it was closing some aluminum beverage canmaking capacity in the U.S.
"We are not complacent. We are aggressive in that arena in terms of protection of our market," Parker said.

But the association, which represents the $30 billion a year aluminum production sector supplying over nine million tonnes of primary and secondary metal, is looking at growth prospects in the automotive industry in the same way as the can was looked upon in the 1970s.
The average U.S. car contains 252 lbs of aluminum, up 61 lbs from five years ago, with forecasts of cars containing 350 to 450 lbs each within five years being taken seriously by the association.

In the meantime, smelters may be faced with rising costs to meet environmental Clean Air Act requirements, the timetable for which will be finalised late this year to early 1998 by the Environmental Protection Agency.
"We anticipate that for some companies to comply with the law will need some significant investments," Parker said.
